Hook: In the early 2000s the economist Benjamin Olken wanted to know how much of the money for new roads in Indonesian villages was stolen. Over 600 villages were building a road. When each road was finished, he sent engineers to dig core samples out of it, to estimate how much sand, rock and gravel was really in it, and what the materials and the labour would have cost. The gap between that and what the village reported spending is money that went missing. More than a fifth of it, on average. Then he tested two cures, drawn at random: an audit from above, by government auditors, and village meetings from below, where the money had to be accounted for in front of the people it was meant for.

The Island runs the same experiment on 600 of its own road projects. Where there is neither an audit nor a meeting, 28 percent of the money is missing. An audit, announced in advance, cuts that by 8.0 points. Meetings move it by 2.5, with a standard error of 1.5: hardly at all. The planted truths were eight points and one, and the trial recovers them. Chapter seven comes back to what Olken found in Indonesia, and why the cure from below did so little.

So this part asks why governments so often choose policies that economists can show are wasteful. Why do small groups win policies that cost everyone else more than they gain? What do voters control, and what do lobbies buy? How can anyone measure what is hidden, like corruption, and what cuts it? And why do bad institutions last, and what makes a state able to act at all?
Economics, Built. Part forty-seven: political economy.

Here is the plan. Why small groups organize and large ones do not, a game for you to play, and the waste of chasing rents. Voters, with the real record of close Senate elections; lobbies and the regulators they capture; and politicians as agents of voters. Audits, four ways of measuring corruption, and why bad institutions last. The capacity of states, democracy and growth, conflict, the media, and economic cycles timed to elections. Two dials, the people who use these ideas, and the frontier.
Collective: Chapter one. The logic of collective action.

In 1965 Mancur Olson pointed out something odd about groups. A policy may be worth a great deal to a group as a whole, and yet the group may do nothing to get it. Here is a policy worth 100 to a group, which wins it with a probability that rises with how hard the group lobbies against fixed resistance. Each member decides how much to put in, and weighs only their own share of the gain, while bearing all of their own cost. Every member hopes the others will do the work. A group of one puts in 9. A group of ten, 2.2 in total. A group of 100 or more, nothing at all, though the policy is worth just as much to it. That is free riding, and it grows with the size of the group. Olson's conclusion: small groups with a lot at stake per head organize; large groups with a little at stake per head do not, unless something else, a membership benefit, a law, forces them to.

The classic example is sugar in the United States. Here is the price of sugar in America, from the World Bank's monthly price data, 1960 to 2026. And the price of sugar on the world market. In most years the American price is about twice the world's: a median of 1.9 times, and 1.9 times on average since 2015. The gap is made in Washington, by import quotas that keep foreign sugar out and loans that put a floor under the price. In 1974 and 1980, when world prices spiked, the two lines met; the rest of the time, Americans pay more.

Who gains and who loses? About four thousand farms grow sugar beet and sugar cane in the United States. The Government Accountability Office reviewed the estimates in 2023: the program is worth about 1.4 to 2.7 billion dollars a year to producers. Per farm, that is hundreds of thousands of dollars. Consumers lose about 2.5 to 3.5 billion. Per American, about nine dollars a year. So the country as a whole loses about 1 billion dollars a year. But nobody writes to their senator about nine dollars, and every sugar farmer has a reason to. Put the two groups into the kind of contest chapter three builds, each lobbying by its stake per head, and the quota survives almost for certain, though it costs consumers more than it gives farmers. Olson called it the exploitation of the great by the small.
PlayIt: Chapter two. Play it: build or lobby?

Your turn. You are one of 10 players, each with 100 tokens. A token you keep is worth one to you. A token you put into building, a road, a school, returns 0.3 to every one of the 10 players, so it is worth three to the group, but only 0.3 to you. A token you spend on lobbying buys you a share of a prize of 400 tokens: the government's favours, divided in proportion to how much each player lobbied. If nobody lobbies, the prize is shared equally.
Pause, and split your hundred tokens: how many do you keep, how many do you build with, and how many do you spend on lobbying?

Here is what happens. If everyone builds, everyone ends with 340 tokens: the building triples, and the prize is shared equally. But look at a society where half build and half lobby. The builders end with 150; the lobbyists, who keep their tokens and take the whole prize, with 294. Each player does better by lobbying than by building, whatever the others do, so building collapses. In equilibrium nobody builds, everyone lobbies 36 tokens, and each ends with 104: barely more than they started with. 360 tokens are spent to win a prize of 400. That is rent seeking, and the next chapter takes it apart.
Rents: Economists used to measure the cost of a monopoly, a tariff or a licence by a small triangle. A privilege raises the price above cost. The units no longer bought are a loss to society: Harberger's triangle, usually small. The rest, the rectangle, is not a loss but a transfer: buyers pay more, and the holder of the privilege collects it. In 1967 Gordon Tullock pointed out that privileges are not handed out for free. If firms compete to win the licence, with lobbyists, lawyers and favours, they will spend up to what it is worth. Then the rectangle is wasted too, and the true cost of the privilege is the triangle and the rectangle together.

Tullock's own contest makes this exact. Each of n players spends something, and wins the prize with probability equal to their share of all the spending, as in the game you just played. In equilibrium each spends the prize times n minus one over n squared, so all together they spend the prize times n minus one over n. With two players, half the prize is spent chasing it. With ten, ninety percent. With many, nearly all of it. Competition, which in a market drives prices down to cost, here drives spending up to the value of the prize.

How big are the rectangles? In 1974 Anne Krueger, who coined the phrase rent seeking, estimated them for two economies run by licences. In India in 1964, rents created by government regulation were about 7.3 percent of national income; import restrictions alone, 5.1 percent. In Turkey in 1968, import licences alone created rents of about 15 percent of national output. She did not estimate how much of those rents was spent chasing them. But if even part of it was, the cost of the licence system was far larger than any triangle.
Voters: Part eighteen's median voter theorem says that with one issue, two parties both move to the voter in the middle. Real voters care about many things, a party's leader, its record, its values, so a promise of money moves only some of them: the swing voters. Here are three groups on the Island, the poor, the middle and the rich, and two parties offering transfers paid for by everyone. The middle group has twice as many swing voters as the others. Both parties end up offering it the most: in this model of probabilistic voting, a group gets more the more of its votes are up for grabs, here a transfer worth 51 percent of average income, paid for mostly by the rich. Policy follows not need, and not numbers, but how easily a group's votes can be bought.

Do voters change what politicians do, or only choose between politicians who will do what they always meant to? David Lee, Enrico Moretti and Matthew Butler used close elections, where who wins is almost a coin toss, and compared House districts that a party barely won with districts it barely lost: a regression discontinuity, as in Part four. If politicians moved toward voters when their seat was marginal, how they voted in Congress would depend on how strong the other party was. It did not. Voters elect policies; they do not affect them, because a candidate cannot credibly promise to vote against their own beliefs once elected.

Close elections also measure what winning is worth. Here are real data: 1,297 elections to the United States Senate between 1914 and 2004, compiled by Matias Cattaneo, Brigham Frandsen and Rocío Titiunik. Across, the Democrats' margin of victory or defeat; up the side, their share of the vote when the same seat next comes up, six years later. Each dot averages the elections in a band two and a half points wide. Fit a line on each side, within 17.8 points of zero, weighting the closest races most. At zero the lines jump by 7.41 points, with a standard error of 1.46. That is the incumbent party's advantage: barely winning a seat, rather than barely losing it, is worth about seven points of the vote six years later. The same calculation in the rdrobust software these data come with gives the same number.

A regression discontinuity has one choice that matters: how far from zero to look. Look only at the very closest races, and there are few of them, so the estimate is noisy. Look further, and there are more races, but they are less alike, and the straight lines must do more work. Across sensible choices the jump stays near seven or eight points, falling a little as the window widens. For the House, David Lee found about the same. Devin Caughey and Jasjeet Sekhon later showed that in the House, bare winners and bare losers differ in ways visible before the election, which suggests the true advantage there is smaller. The second dial of chapter fourteen collects these.
Capture: Olson's logic has a sharp consequence for regulation. A regulator is set up to protect the public from an industry. But the industry knows far more about its business than anyone else, and cares far more about the rules. The regulator needs its expertise, and its staff may one day want its jobs. So rules drift toward the industry's interest: licences that keep out entrants, prices held up. In 1971 George Stigler put it bluntly: as a rule, regulation is acquired by the industry, and designed and operated primarily for its benefit. He called it capture.

Add money to chapter four's model. In grey, the transfers when only voters count. Now let the rich organize, as a lobby: they give money to whichever party promises them more, and the money buys advertising that wins votes elsewhere. In the parties' arithmetic, the organized group now counts as if it had many more swing voters. The rich, who paid 84 percent of average income, now pay 35 percent, and the middle's gain shrinks from 51 to 25 percent. Nothing about the groups' needs changed, only who was organized.

Part thirty-five met this in trade policy. In Gene Grossman and Elhanan Helpman's model, a government weighs the contributions of organized industries against the welfare of everyone. It predicts more protection for industries that are organized, produce much and import little, and whose imports barely respond to price, where protection costs the least welfare. When Pinelopi Goldberg and Giovanni Maggi fitted it to American tariffs and quotas, the weight on welfare came out 50 to 88 times the weight on money. The government was mostly benevolent. It sold protection anyway, because at the margin a little protection costs everyone a little and pays a few a lot: Olson's arithmetic again.

How much is a political connection worth? Raymond Fisman found a way to price it. In the last years of President Suharto's rule in Indonesia, consultants ranked firms by how closely they were tied to the president and his family. Several times, rumours spread that Suharto was gravely ill. Each time, the shares of the most connected firms fell further than the shares of the rest. Investors were telling him how much of each firm's value depended on the president staying alive: for the best-connected, a large share. The stock market, it turns out, is a corruption meter.
Agency: Robert Barro in 1973 and John Ferejohn in 1986 treated politicians as agents of the voters, like the managers of Part fourteen. Voters hire a politician, but cannot watch everything they do. In office, the politician could take rents, up to some amount R a term, by graft, favours or slacking. Voters re-elect only if rents stay below a threshold. The politician complies if keeping office, term after term, is worth more than one big grab followed by defeat. So the lowest threshold voters can enforce is one minus delta, times W plus R, minus W: smaller when office pays well and when the future counts. And a politician who cannot run again, a lame duck, has nothing to lose, and takes R.

Here is the threshold, for rents of up to one a term. Across, what a term in office is worth to the politician; up the side, the rents voters must tolerate to keep them honest. The three lines are politicians who weigh the future less or more. The more office pays, and the more the future counts, the less voters have to tolerate, until it reaches zero. It is Part fourteen's efficiency wage, applied to the state: a job worth keeping is a job not worth risking.

The model predicts that lame ducks steal more. On the Island, 2,000 towns have mayors who differ in how much they value office and in honesty. First-term mayors can run again; second-term mayors are barred. Audits find that first-term mayors misappropriate 29 percent less. Brazil ran this experiment for real. Its federal government audited municipal spending in towns chosen by lottery, and mayors were limited to two terms. Claudio Ferraz and Frederico Finan found that mayors who could run again misappropriated 27 percent less than mayors in their last term. A replication published in 2025, with more years of audits, finds a smaller effect for the same period, and almost none in later terms. Accountability works, but less reliably than the first study suggested.
Audits: Chapter seven. Audits from above, meetings from below.

Here is what Olken found in Indonesia. In projects that faced the usual small chance of an audit, 27.7 percent of the money was missing, by J-PAL's summary of the study. In projects told, before construction began, that they would certainly be audited, 19.2 percent. About 8 points less, and the money saved was more than the audits cost. Village meetings and anonymous comment forms did little on average. They reduced missing wages, which villagers could see because they or their neighbours had worked on the road, but not missing materials, which they could not.

Why did monitoring from below fail? Free riding: every villager gains from a well-built road, but each gains little from spending an evening checking the accounts, chapter one's logic at the scale of a village. Visibility: villagers can see who was paid, but not how much gravel lies under the asphalt. Capture: meetings can be dominated by the same village elite who manage the money; participation reduced theft only where free riding and elite capture were limited. And credibility: an auditor's report can lead to prosecution, while a neighbour can only complain.

Olken also asked the villagers how corrupt they thought their road project was. Their answers tracked the truth only faintly: ten percent more money missing made a villager 0.8 percent more likely to think there was any corruption at all, partly because officials hid the theft where villagers could not see it. In ethnically mixed villages people perceived more corruption, and there was less. The Island's villagers are planted the same way: the correlation between what they perceive and what is stolen is 0.15. That matters, because most of what the world knows about corruption comes from surveys of perceptions. The next chapters measure it four ways.
Measure: Chapter eight. Corruption measured four ways.

Corruption is hidden on purpose, so economists measure it indirectly. First, physical audits: compare what was built with what was paid for, as Olken's engineers did. Second, prices: Fisman's share prices, which priced the value of a connection. Third, behaviour where nothing forces honesty. Until 2002, diplomats at the United Nations in New York could ignore parking tickets, because of diplomatic immunity. Raymond Fisman and Edward Miguel found that diplomats from countries with more corruption at home ran up many more unpaid tickets: norms travel with people. Fourth, surveys of what firms, citizens and experts say they see or pay. Each has its blind spots; together they agree on more than any one alone.

A fifth way is to follow the money. In the early 1990s Uganda's central government sent grants for every primary-school pupil, through district officials. Ritva Reinikka and Jakob Svensson surveyed schools to see what actually arrived. In the mid-1990s, about one-fifth: on average, schools received only 13 percent of the grants between 1991 and 1995. Then the government began publishing the monthly transfers to each district in the newspapers, so that head teachers and parents knew what to expect, and the share reaching schools rose sharply. Information worked here where meetings had not in Indonesia: it told people exactly what to look for.

The most widely used measure is built from surveys. The World Bank's Worldwide Governance Indicators combine dozens of surveys of firms, households and experts into one estimate of how well each country controls corruption. Here it is for 195 countries, against income. The correlation is 0.72: rich countries are seen as cleaner. But which causes which? Corruption may keep countries poor, growth may pay for honest institutions, and, as Olken found, perceptions may simply follow appearances. The countries far above the line, cleaner than their incomes predict, such as Rwanda and Botswana, are where economists look for what institutions and reforms can do.
Persist: Chapter nine. Why bad institutions persist.

Why do institutions that make most people poorer survive, and why do they sometimes change? Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson put the problem as one of commitment. An elite rules, and most people are poor. Now and then, in a war, a slump or a bad harvest, the poor could organize and overthrow it. The elite can promise to share: lower taxes for the poor, schools, land. But once the crisis passes, the elite holds power again and can take the promise back, and the poor know it. Extending the vote solves this. Once the poor can vote, redistribution no longer depends on the elite's word. That is why, they argue, elites in nineteenth-century Europe extended the franchise when the threat of unrest was high.

Here it is on the Island. The richest 10 percent earn 70 percent of income. A revolution would destroy sixty percent of the economy, but the poor would keep the rest, forever: the red line is what that is worth to them. If crises come one year in ten, the elite's promises, honoured only during crises, are worth 7.3, less than revolution. If crises come nine years in ten, the promises keep being renewed, and are worth 10.7, enough. The vote, which makes redistribution permanent, is worth 11.1. So where crises are rare, an elite facing one must give up the vote to survive; where they are frequent, it can get by on promises. The paradox: it is the elite that is only occasionally threatened that democratizes.

The whole picture, across how often crises come and how costly a revolution is. Where revolution is cheap, nothing the elite can offer stops it. Where it is costlier, but crises are rare, the elite extends the vote. Where crises are frequent, or revolution very costly, promises are enough, and the old institutions survive. Acemoglu and Robinson read Britain's reform acts of 1832, 1867 and 1884, each passed amid unrest, this way. The model also explains why reforms that would make everyone richer are blocked: an elite that cannot be compensated credibly for what it would lose will resist them.
State: Chapter ten. State capacity and democracy.

Most of this part has been about states that do the wrong thing. Timothy Besley and Torsten Persson asked why many states cannot do much at all. To tax, a state needs registers of firms and people, withholding at source, inspectors: fiscal capacity. To protect property and enforce contracts, it needs courts that work: legal capacity. Both must be built in advance, by governments that will not necessarily be the ones to use them. So states invest when there is a common interest, such as a war that threatens everyone, when politics is stable, and when institutions include enough people that whoever rules next will not turn the capacity against them. The two capacities reinforce each other.

One trace of fiscal capacity is how much a state collects. Here is tax revenue as a share of GDP for 150 countries, from the World Bank's data, against income. In the poorest quarter of countries the median central government collects 13 percent of GDP; in the richest quarter, 22 percent. These are central government taxes only; add social insurance contributions and local taxes, and rich countries collect much more. Poor states cannot tax much of their economies, which are informal and paid in cash, and so cannot pay for the schools, roads and courts that would make them richer.

Does democracy itself make a country richer? Here are seven countries that became democracies in the last third of the twentieth century, by the V-Dem project's index: Spain after Franco, Chile after Pinochet, South Korea, Poland, Taiwan, Ghana and Indonesia. Each jumps within a few years from the bottom of the scale to near the top. Comparing their incomes before and after is not enough, because countries often democratize in a crisis, and grow for many other reasons.

Daron Acemoglu, Suresh Naidu, Pascual Restrepo and James Robinson tried to make the comparison fair. They used a panel of countries from 1960, comparing those that democratized with similar countries that did not, and allowing for the economic slump that often comes just before a transition. They found GDP per head about 20 percent higher 25 years after a democratization, with similar answers from other methods. Democracies, they argue, invest more, school more of their people, provide more public goods, reform more, and suffer less unrest. The gains come slowly, which is part of why democracy is hard to defend in its first years.
Conflict: Poor countries have far more civil wars than rich ones. Does poverty cause war? Or does war cause poverty? Both, surely, which is why a simple correlation proves nothing. Edward Miguel, Shanker Satyanath and Ernest Sergenti looked for something that moves incomes but not conflict directly, and found it in the rain: in Africa, where most farming depends on it, a dry year means a poor year. Using rainfall as an instrument for growth, as in Part four, they found that a fall in growth of five percent raised the risk of civil conflict in the following year by up to ten percentage points, nearly half.

The Island has 41 countries followed for 19 years, with the planted effect: a fall in growth of five points raises the risk of conflict by ten. In grey, the truth. Growth in poor countries is measured badly, here with an error of 4 points, and that drags a least-squares estimate toward zero: minus 1.51. Rainfall moves true growth, and has nothing to do with the statistician's errors, so the instrumental estimate recovers the effect: minus 1.97, with a standard error of 0.47. An instrument is only as good as its assumption: that rain affects conflict only through incomes. And later work found the link between rain and growth in Africa weaker after 2000, so the instrument itself has grown weaker.

Natural resources can make conflict worse. In 1995 Jeffrey Sachs and Andrew Warner found that countries whose exports were mostly natural resources in 1971 grew more slowly over the next two decades, even with other influences on growth held fixed. The political reasons: oil and diamonds are rents worth fighting over, and a state that lives on them needs no taxpayers, so it answers to none. The economic reason, the Dutch disease: resource exports strengthen the currency and crowd out other exports. But the curse is not a law. Measured by reserves rather than exports, it weakens, and Norway and Botswana turned resources into prosperity, through institutions that came first.
Media: Do the media change minds, or only tell people what they already think? In 1996 a new cable channel, Fox News, was launched. Cable companies added it town by town, and by the 2000 election some towns had it and others did not. Stefano DellaVigna and Ethan Kaplan argued that which towns got it early had little to do with their politics, and compared the change in the Republican vote between 1996 and 2000 in towns with the channel and without. The Republican share rose by 0.4 to 0.7 points more where Fox had arrived. In a country where one presidential election that year was decided by a few hundred votes, that is not small.

A small change in votes can hide a large effect on the people who watched. DellaVigna and Kaplan turned their estimate into a persuasion rate. Take the difference in the vote between places with and without the message, divide by the difference in how many people received it, and divide again by the share who were not already voting that way. In an Island town where the party's share is 50.4 percent against 50.0, and 30 percent of homes get the channel against 20, the persuasion rate is 8 percent. For Fox News, between 3 and 28 percent of viewers who were not already Republican were persuaded, depending on how the audience is measured, and 3 to 8 percent with the broadest measures. Persuasion rates like these turn up in studies of advertising, canvassing and news alike.

Economic shocks move politics too. Part thirty-six measured the China shock: the surge of Chinese imports into the United States after 2001. David Autor, David Dorn, Gordon Hanson and Kaveh Majlesi followed it into elections. In the congressional districts most exposed, where factories closed, voters removed moderate representatives between 2002 and 2010, replacing them with more conservative Republicans in mostly white districts and more liberal Democrats elsewhere. Exposed areas also watched more Fox News. The authors call the evidence strong though not definitive, and note that American polarization did not begin with China. But a trade shock, with no politics in it, left a political mark.
Frontier: Chapter sixteen. Frontier: populism, and the digital state.

The first frontier is a reversal. After 1990, the world's average on V-Dem's index rose for two decades, and has fallen since about 2012. Some countries moved back a long way: Hungary, Turkey, Venezuela and Russia, each led for years by leaders who won elections and then weakened the courts, the press and the opposition. Economists are trying to understand why voters support this, and what it costs.

What does populism cost? Manuel Funke, Moritz Schularick and Christoph Trebesch assembled 51 populist presidents and prime ministers, from 1900 to 2020, defining populists as leaders who claim to speak for the people against a corrupt elite, whether from the left or the right. Fifteen years after such a leader takes office, GDP per head is about 10 percent below a comparable path without one. The losses come with less trade, less stable macroeconomic policy, and weaker institutions. Why voters choose such leaders anyway, after crises, trade shocks and the rest of this part's forces, is the open question.

The second frontier is the digital state. In the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh, payments for a public employment programme and for pensions passed through local officials, and much of the money leaked. The state introduced biometric smartcards, paid out by local agents, and Karthik Muralidharan, Paul Niehaus and Sandip Sukhtankar evaluated the roll-out, randomized across 157 sub-districts with about 19 million people. Payments became faster and more predictable, and beneficiaries preferred the new system. Leakage fell significantly, and the time saved alone was worth about what the system cost. State capacity, in this frontier, is built from identity systems, digital payments and records, which raise their own questions about privacy, and about who gets left out.
